To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified the HBV DNA integrant in a human hepatoma cell and analyzed the viral-cellular breakpoint by IPCR.

by using conventional PCR to choose the nearest restriction site for the inverse PCR (IPCP) to clone the junction sequence of the integrated HB virus DNA and the human hepatoma cellular gene, a higher successful rate of cloning and analysis was obtained.

by choosing the restriction sites nearest to the integrated viral sequence, which can be identified by conventional PCR, the successful rate of IPCR is higher than that of using a unique restriction site within the integrated virus to clone the flanking sequence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of HBsAg-positive hepatoma cell line HAGS 1.1, which is the first hepatoma cell line to express hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and to be established in Taiwan.
the molecular biology of the integration site of HBV in human hepatoma cell lines and the mechanism of HBV integration into the human genome.
the analysis of HBsAg production in HAGS2.1 cells and the molecular mechanism of the integration of HBV DNA in human liver cancer cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the integrated HBV in HAGS cells is a truncated form of HBV genome, and the cellular sequence is a human satellite III sequence.
the HBV integrations in HAGS cells are not random and the integration site of the HBV DNA is not random.
the HBV DNA in the HAGS 1.1 cell line is not integrated with the cellular gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
by using the IPCR technique, the viral-cellular integration sites of HAGS 1.1 and HAGS 3.3 cells have been identified and characterized.
the HBV integration in HAGS cells is not a simple random integration but is a site-directed integration.
by using a combination of conventional PCR and IPCR, it is possible to identify the viral-cellular sequence in a cell line and to clone and sequence the junction sequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by using the combination of IPCR and conventional PCR, it is feasible to identify and characterize the junction between viral and cellular genes.
by combining conventional PCR with IPCR, it is possible to clone the junction sequence between the integrated viral DNA and its cellular counterpart.
the combination of conventional PCR and IPCR is a powerful method for the analysis of integrated viral sequences.
